newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: FEATURE-Life after death for Trabant in Tashkent?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Life after death for Trabant in Tashkent?.

text.p: When East Germany died in 1990 it was not long before its trademark Trabant car followed. But now, thousands of miles and a post-communist world away, the tiny box on wheels may be coming back to life.

"We have both the money and potential to reach a production level of 30,000-40,000 Trabants a year within six months," said Vyacheslav Shin, deputy head of U.S.-Uzbek joint venture Olimp, which plans to build the car in Uzbekistan's capital, Tashkent.

Its enthusiastic backers readily dismiss the sarcasm which East Europeans now heap on the lowly Trabant -- which has a sewing machine-style engine concealed inside an angular body with the aerodynamics of a brick.
"This car is not ultra-modern," Shin told Reuters. "But it is cheap and simple. Residents of Uzbekistan and neighbouring states are showing great interest in it."

The venture, in which the U.S. partner holds a 55 percent stake, has been set up with initial capital of around $1 million and boasts a team prepared to lavish just as much affection on the car as a whole generation of East Germans did before the Berlin Wall fell in 1989.
Uzbek government hard currency restrictions have delayed the start of production and it is unclear when the Trabants will start to roll. But roll they will, according to Shin.
GLASS FIBRE IS OUT, COTTON IS IN FOR TRABANT BODY

Last year, when presenting the first, light-green sample of the 26-horsepower Trabant -- assembled at an experimental plant in Tashkent -- Shin jumped on its roof to show reporters and onlookers how solid it was.

With a nod to the specific character of the Uzbek economy, Olimp plans to produce Trabant bodies not from "Duroplast" -- old East Germany's answer to glass fibre -- but from pressed waste from the Central Asian republic's cotton output.
Uzbek Trabants would retail in Uzbekistan at $1,800-$3,000, depending on their modifications, Shin said.
Salaries in Uzbekistan, a largely desert state with a population of 23 million, average just $20 a month. But Shin said Trabants would find buyers even in this impoverished republic.

Last year, Uzbekistan -- already dubbed an "automobile country" by the official press -- launched its UzDAEWOOavto joint venture with South Korea's industrial conglomerate Daewoo in the town of Asaka in the eastern Fergana region.

The venture with a capital of $658 million has produced some 60,000 Nexia sedans, Tico mini-cars and Damas mini-buses since March last year, and plans to reach annual production of 200,000 cars by the year 2000.
UzDAEWOOavto's products sell for around $7,500.
But Olimp's Trabant devotees see a bright future for their car, more than six years after the last model rolled off the assembly line in the East German town of Zwickau.
"We will never part with our dream. We are not competitors for Daewoo," said Shin, confident the resurrected Trabant would find its consumer niche.
He said countries of the former Soviet Union could buy at least 10,000 cars a year, and there were already orders from Bulgaria, Romania and China.

Trabants are still seen spluttering round the streets of eastern Germany, and have acquired something of a cult "retro" status. But many have been scrapped in favour of more environmentally-friendly Western cars.
Shin said Olimp could easily produce 200,000 Trabants within five years, giving a fossil of the former Communist car industry a new lease of life.
ENTHUSIASM BUT NOT PLAIN SAILING
But just as production was about to start toward the tail-end of last year, the Uzbek government's economic policy shoved an unexpected spanner into the works.
A multiple exchange-rate mechanism and restrictions imposed last year on currency convertibility prompted the International Monetary Fund to suspend loans to Uzbekistan.
For Shin, this meant a delay in launching his dream.

In mid-1996, Sachsenring GmBH, the successor to the East German firm that used to build Trabants, gave Olimp the licence and technological information necessary to produce the first 5,000 Trabants from parts to be brought from Germany.

Germany's investment agency Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau agreed last year to lend a total of 15 million marks ($8 million) to Olimp to help launch the production of the first 5,000 Trabants but the deal was blocked by new currency rules.
"Our idea finds support in the government, but we hear only promises. Convertibility is a political issue. Even large investors face similar problems," Shin complained.
Shin is also concerned about Olimp's fading image in Zwickau, which used to produce Trabants before East and West Germany merged in 1990.
"The owners of Sachsenring in Zwickau do not view us in the best light now. We had a good chance to produce a qualitatively new model of the Trabant," he said.
But despite present-day troubles, Trabant enthusiasts keep the faith with a car that has quite a history.
"This odd-looking car has a future," said a car fitter working near a garage. Inside sits Uzbekistan's sole example so far of a home-produced Trabant. ($ = 1.865 German Marks)
